pieces.title: The key photo was not seen from the prize podium: Rosalind Franklin
pieces.hook: Turn an image into evidence no one can ignore: a model can be argued over, but a photo puts the fact of the helix on the table.
pieces.takeaway: Turn an image into evidence no one can ignore: a model can be argued over, but a photo puts the fact of the helix on the table.
pieces.imageCredit: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (MRC LMB) · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958) was a British physical chemist and crystallographer. The DNA double helix made it into textbooks partly thanks to an X-ray diffraction photo she helped take.
Yet her name was not among the Nobel laureates of 1962.

She was born on 25 July 1920 into a Jewish family in London. She read natural sciences at Newnham College, Cambridge, graduated in 1941, and earned her PhD in 1945 for research on coal and carbon materials. From 1947 to 1950 she learned X-ray diffraction in Paris, and this way of seeing microscopic structure became her sharpest tool.

In January 1951 she joined King's College London and, with graduate student Raymond Gosling, took fibre diffraction images of DNA. Maurice Wilkins was already working on nucleic acids in the lab; the two sides understood their roles and collaboration differently, and trust never developed.
In May 1952 they took the image later known as "Photo 51": it pointed clearly to a helical structure and gave key dimensions.

paras.lead: How the photo came to be seen
parts: In January 1953 Wilkins showed "Photo 51" to the visiting James Watson, without Franklin knowing beforehand. Around the same time, a report she had written for the Medical Research Council reached Crick through someone else. Watson and Crick sped up their model building.

On 25 April 1953, Nature published three papers in one issue: Watson and Crick proposed the double helix, while Wilkins's group and Franklin and Gosling each presented experimental evidence. Her paper was not labelled as a mere "supplement", yet the pair who built the model are the ones most often remembered.

In March 1953 she moved to Birkbeck College, applied her method to tobacco mosaic virus and then poliovirus, and produced structural work her peers valued. In 1956 she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer, yet kept experimenting and writing.
She died in London on 16 April 1958, aged only 37.

paras.lead: The prize went to the living
parts: In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on nucleic acid structure. The Nobel is not awarded posthumously, so she could not have been chosen. Later historians focused on whether key data were used properly, and how credit should have been shared had she lived.
Her work on virus structure was carried on by colleagues including Aaron Klug, who won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

items: Three papers in the same issue of Nature
Related Nobel goes to three others
Moves to Birkbeck; DNA paper published

critical.label: Another angle
items: Franklin｜View: A structure must first be measured reliably.；Interest: Reaching her own conclusions from first-hand data.；Worry: Materials, equipment and priority being shared without clear rules.；Basis: She insisted on high-quality diffraction images and wrote her 1953 paper independently.

Watson and Crick｜View: Use available clues to build, as fast as possible, a model that explains replication.；Interest: Priority for the correct structure.；Worry: Being beaten by another lab.；Basis: Their 1953 double-helix paper; they later acknowledged using King's College data.

Wilkins｜View: DNA research at King's was one shared line of work.；Interest: Not having his own lab sidelined.；Worry: The division of labour with Franklin was never settled.；Basis: He showed "Photo 51" to Watson; he shared the 1962 Nobel Prize.

The Nobel system and later storytelling｜View: The prize goes only to the living, and to a limited number.；Interest: Honouring "discovery" and forming a simple heroic story.；Worry: Turning the experimenter into a supporting character.；Basis: The statutes do not allow posthumous awards; the public later retold the story through "Photo 51".

Colleagues in virology and structural biology｜View: Her later virus work matters just as much.；Interest: Extending X-ray methods to larger living structures.；Worry: The DNA story overshadowing other contributions.；Basis: Her tobacco mosaic virus research; Klug's later prize.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: Without that photo the model would have come far more slowly; without the model, the photo alone would not have explained base pairing.
Data used without her consent sped up the discovery and left an ethical controversy.
Her early death kept her out of the next twenty years of credit-sharing.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The discovery was clearly the work of several labs and several kinds of evidence, yet the honours system tends to remember only the two people who built the model.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Whether Wilkins thought he was entitled to share his lab's material when he showed the photo is something the people involved later described differently.
Historians still differ slightly on how close Franklin was to reaching the helix conclusion on her own.
Some vivid anecdotes about everyday discrimination in the lab come from sources of mixed quality; this article uses only firmer facts about institutions and papers.

pieces.title: One shot instead of a deadly disease: two hundred years of vaccines
pieces.hook: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated.
pieces.imageAlt: Jenner vaccinating Phipps with cowpox (oil painting)
pieces.imageCredit: Ernest Board · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated. It was the first time humans had wiped a highly dangerous infectious disease out of nature. This came not from a miracle drug but from turning vaccination into a public system that could cover a whole population.

Before Jenner, places such as China and West Asia already practised "variolation": inoculating people with material from smallpox pustules to make the illness milder, at considerable risk. On 14 May 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with cowpox, later challenged him with smallpox matter, and the boy did not fall ill.
The method was safer and spread across Europe and beyond; the word "vaccine" comes from it.

paras.lead: From one disease to a whole technology
parts: In 1885 Pasteur used his rabies vaccine on a child bitten by a rabid dog, showing that vaccination could even race the clock after exposure. Vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, tuberculosis, yellow fever and more followed. In the mid-20th century, inactivated and live attenuated polio vaccines lifted polio out of everyday fear in many countries.
Vaccines stopped being folk remedies and became an industrial and public-health system of standardised production, cold-chain transport and scheduled immunisation.

After the founding of the People's Republic, China gradually rolled out BCG, smallpox, measles and other vaccinations. In 1978 it began planned immunisation, first using "four vaccines" against six diseases and making vaccination part of routine health services. In 1988, 1990 and 1996 the four vaccines reached the 85% coverage target at provincial, county and township level respectively; today the township-level target has been raised to 90%.
The point of planned immunisation: a vaccine becomes a public good only when enough children receive it on time and on schedule.

The 21st century brought conjugate vaccines, genetically engineered vaccines and new platforms such as the mRNA vaccines used at scale during COVID-19, sharply shortening development for some vaccines. Meanwhile cold chains, patents, unequal distribution and vaccine refusal became as important as the lab.

Smallpox could be eradicated because it has no animal host, its symptoms are easy to recognise, and vaccination was sustained worldwide; many diseases lack those conditions. What vaccines can do is add up "one person's shot" into "a whole group's barrier". Loosen that barrier and old diseases come back.

items: Four-vaccine coverage reaches 85% at provincial, county, then township level

critical.label: Another angle
items: Vaccinated people and parents｜View: Want children to avoid deadly or disabling diseases.；Interest: Personal health, plus a share of the group barrier.；Worry: Side effects, and "everyone else is vaccinated, so I can skip it".；Basis: High coverage is the precondition for elimination; when coverage drops, outbreaks can return.

Vaccine developers and manufacturers｜View: Turn antigens into products that can be made at scale with quality control.；Interest: Returns on R&D, and markets.；Worry: Long timelines, heavy liability, demand that rises and falls with epidemics.；Basis: The shift from workshop preparation to industrial production and cold-chain transport.

Public-health authorities｜View: Vaccination must be a routine system, not a one-off campaign.；Interest: Lowering the burden of infectious disease.；Worry: Funding, access in remote areas, and refusal.；Basis: China's planned immunisation made coverage a measurable target.

International health bodies｜View: Some diseases end only if the whole world vaccinates together.；Interest: Eliminating or blocking cross-border spread.；Worry: Conflict, funding cuts and vaccine nationalism.；Basis: Smallpox eradication relied on sustained vaccination and surveillance in many countries.

Sceptics and opponents of vaccination｜View: Stress individual choice and rare harms.；Interest: Refusing risks they consider unnecessary.；Worry: Being compelled.；Basis: There have been substandard vaccines and communication failures; but inflating single cases into rejecting a whole technology reopens doors that had been closed.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: Vaccines benefit people who never get sick, while side effects happen to visible individuals, which makes public communication inherently hard.
Patents and capacity encourage R&D, but in a crisis can also push poorer countries to the back of the queue.
New platforms speed up response, but "not yet fully tested by time" becomes a new point of dispute.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A lab can produce a shot quickly, but without trust, cold chains and coverage, doses do not become a barrier.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The exact date when variolation began in China is still debated in the records and their interpretation.
Some early coverage figures for planned immunisation were counted against the targets of the time and differ from today's monitoring methods.
Long-term data on different new-platform vaccines are still accumulating; no single number sums up their overall effect.

pieces.title: Revenue up only a tenth, shares up 14% in a day: design firm Stantec's third quarter
pieces.hook: After the US market closed on Thursday 12 November, Canadian engineering and design consultancy Stantec reported…
pieces.event: 2026-11-12 (Edmonton) Q3 results released after the US close; 11-13 shares closed up 14.06% in New York

parts: After the US market closed on Thursday 12 November, Canadian engineering and design consultancy Stantec reported its third quarter: net revenue of C$1.865 billion, up 9.4% year on year, and adjusted earnings per share of C$1.89, up 23.5%. The next day it closed at US$85.69 on the New York Stock Exchange, up 14.06% in a single day (closing data cited by Motley Fool).

In 1954 Don Stanley, freshly armed with a Harvard doctorate in environmental engineering, started D.R. Stanley Associates on his own in an office of about 23 square metres in Edmonton. Seventy-odd years later it has more than 450 locations on six continents and about 34,000 employees, organised into five businesses: water, infrastructure, buildings, environmental services, and energy & resources.
It doesn't build towers or pave roads; it sells engineers' and designers' time and judgment.

Gross revenue this quarter was C$2.353 billion, but part of it is money paid to subconsultants, equipment and so on that is recovered directly from clients, and it varies a lot by contract. So the company focuses on "net revenue": gross revenue minus subconsultant and other direct costs.
Of the growth in net revenue to C$1.865 billion, 5.3 percentage points came from the existing business (organic growth) and 2.6 points from acquisitions.

It was squeezed from both ends. On one end, "project margin" (net revenue minus direct payroll) rose from 54.4% to 55.0%; on the other, administrative and marketing expenses fell from 36.1% to 35.5% of net revenue. As a result adjusted EBITDA grew 16.6% to C$377.1 million, a 20.2% margin, up 1.2 percentage points.
The company credited solid project execution, favourable recoveries on some projects, and tighter discretionary spending.

At the end of September its signed but unfinished contracts (backlog) stood at C$9.2 billion, up 11.6%, with 9.9% organic growth, roughly 13 months of work. Backlog in Canada and the "Global" region (UK, Australia, New Zealand and others) grew organically by 18.4% and 13.7%.
Of its five businesses, water grew fastest: net revenue of C$510.1 million this quarter, up 11.6%.

The company raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA margin target from 17.8%–18.3% to 18.3%–18.5%, and its adjusted EPS growth target from 15%–18% to 17%–19%; it narrowed net revenue growth to 9%–11%. This quarter it also spent C$174.5 million buying back about 1.72 million shares, and lifted the quarterly dividend from C$0.225 to C$0.245.

Shareholders gain first: profit, buybacks and dividends are all rising. Clients pouring money into water, power and data centres also need design capacity like this. The pressure is in the report too: industrial water, hydropower and dam projects in the US South are winding down; US housing starts are forecast to dip slightly, and the architecture billings index stood at 47.2 in August (below 50 means contraction); days sales outstanding were 76, three more than a year earlier.

The facts: revenue is growing steadily, margins are widening, and orders are growing faster than revenue. The inference: since orders are growing faster than revenue, revenue may accelerate in coming quarters—that is how Motley Fool read it on 13 November.
But that depends on whether public infrastructure budgets and private investment hold up, and the company lists these as risks in its forward-looking statements.

paras.lead: What you can take from it
parts: With companies that "sell time", don't look only at how much revenue grew. Three things matter more: whether each hour of work earns a fatter margin, whether overhead is being spread thinner by scale, and how long the order book will keep the team busy.

blocks.title: Q3 comparison (Canadian dollars)
blocks.note: Figures from Stantec's Q3 2026 Management's Discussion and Analysis (12 November).
rows: Admin & marketing expenses (% of net revenue)

blocks.title: Design firms have caught the data-centre wave too
blocks.text: Among the new projects listed in the report, an unnamed global technology company hired Stantec's Buildings team to design a data-centre facility in Arizona, including equipment yards and two retention and detention basins; growth in Infrastructure also came from data-centre projects in the north central region. Elsewhere, England's Environment Agency selected it for a £17.8 million national groundwater-modelling framework.

items: Don Stanley starts the firm in Edmonton
Reports Q3, raises full-year profit targets

critical.label: Another angle
items: Management｜View: Demand from ageing infrastructure, climate resilience, energy and advanced manufacturing is still there, and margins can keep rising.；Interest: Margin and EPS growth, buybacks.；Worry: Some US South projects winding down; weak housing and building design.；Basis: The "Outlook" section of the 12 November MD&A; raised full-year profit targets the same day (MD&A, canadanewsmedia).

Shareholders and analysts｜View: Orders growing faster than revenue suggest growth may accelerate.；Interest: Valuation and share price.；Worry: Organic growth was only 5.3%; part of the growth comes from acquisitions.；Basis: Motley Fool, 13 Nov: backlog up nearly 12%, faster than sales; shares +14.06% that day.

Public-sector clients｜View: Need design capacity for water, flood defence and transport.；Interest: Projects delivered on budget and on time.；Worry: Whether budgets last.；Basis: England's Environment Agency £17.8 million groundwater-modelling framework; the company calls public infrastructure spending a key growth driver in 2026 (MD&A).

Private tech and energy clients｜View: Data centres, power and factories must get built fast.；Interest: Speed and engineering certainty.；Worry: Design and construction capacity falling behind.；Basis: The Arizona data-centre design project; growth from data-centre projects in Infrastructure (MD&A).

Building and housing markets｜View: Demand for new construction is still contracting.；Interest: Home prices and building costs.；Worry: Interest rates and the economic outlook.；Basis: US architecture billings index 47.2 in August; Canadian new housing construction down 4.0% year on year in September (cited in the MD&A).

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: This quarter's profit expansion came from a lower admin-cost ratio and higher project margin; whether full-year targets are met depends on orders turning into revenue on schedule.
Public clients and private tech clients are both demanding design capacity; as orders grow, staffing and delivery pace become the constraint.
Shareholders focus on order growth, while building and housing markets are still contracting; the two sources of demand point in different directions.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Margins have reached 20.2% and the market is paying for orders and raised targets; but whether orders become revenue on time depends on whether public budgets and private investment weaken, a risk the report itself lists.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: "Orders growing faster than revenue means growth is accelerating" is an analyst's inference, not a company forecast.
The share of data-centre projects in the backlog is not disclosed separately.
How much of the one-day share jump came from results and how much from market mood cannot be separated.

pieces.title: Police who fire, presumed lawful first? France's fifth Saturday on the streets
pieces.short: Police who fire, presumed lawful first?…
pieces.hook: AFP and France 24 reported on 14 November: it was France's fifth nationwide day of protest in a row on a Saturday.
pieces.event: 2026-11-14 (Paris and elsewhere) fifth Saturday of nationwide protests; the Senate is due to debate the police firearms bill on 11-19
pieces.imageAlt: The Statue of the Republic on Place de la République, Paris

parts: AFP and France 24 reported on 14 November: it was France's fifth nationwide day of protest in a row on a Saturday. The interior ministry counted about 106,000 people nationwide, 24,000 of them in Paris; student unions said 200,000, nearly 100,000 in Paris.

It was the smallest turnout in recent weeks, with 219 people detained nationwide. The demands were varied: living costs, school funding, child protection, and a police firearms bill about to go to the Senate.

paras.lead: More than a month on the streets
parts: For more than a month, students have blockaded French high schools, and strikes and marches have kept coming. The biggest was the union strike day on Thursday 5 November, with more than 500,000 people by official count; the previous Saturday (7 November), the official count was about 146,000.
The government promised to raise the minimum wage by 0.6%; unions called it "crumbs" and called a new strike for Tuesday 17 November.

It was proposed by Éric Pauget and other deputies of the right-wing "Droite Républicaine" group and passed by the National Assembly on 7 July 2026. Originally a "presumption of self-defence for police", it was rewritten wholesale in debate: it now presumes that national police officers and gendarmes who use their weapons acted "within the legal framework".

That framework dates from 2017 and sits in Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code: weapons may be used only in cases of "absolute necessity" and in a "strictly proportionate" way, in five listed situations.
The Senate's law committee adopted the text unchanged on 10 November; the rapporteur is Lauriane Josende. Floor debate is scheduled for 19 November and 10 December.

The committee's view: it is only a "simple presumption" that any contrary evidence can overturn; the conditions for firing are unchanged and investigations can still be opened; but when an investigation finds no evidence of misconduct, prosecutors will have firmer grounds to close the case.

The Senate report cites police and gendarmerie inspectorate data: in 2024 police suffered 6,625 physical assaults, 1,289 of them with a weapon; since the start of 2026 nearly 3,200 gendarmes have been injured in assaults, 25% more than a year earlier. Meanwhile police are firing less: "operational shots" at people or vehicles fell from 338 in 2017 to 176 in 2025.
Marine Le Pen's National Rally also backs the bill, arguing it prevents police from being "automatically suspected" of excessive force.

Student groups, unions and human-rights organisations call it a "licence to kill". They fear investigations will be harder to open and accountability harder to secure—AFP notes that in France, alleged police brutality cases rarely reach a criminal court. The independent investigative group Index argues the burden of proof would shift onto victims' families.

A petition against the bill gathered more than 730,000 signatures and was shelved without debate. Lawyers said last week that protesters in recent weeks had suffered hand, foot and eye injuries, and that at least 18 injured people plan to sue the interior ministry.

France elects a president in spring 2027. AFP says Le Pen leads the polls, left-winger Jean-Luc Mélenchon is projected to come second, and the centre-right has yet to find a strong joint candidate; Macron's popularity is at its lowest since 2017, and the government has little room to manoeuvre as it tries to cut debt.
Index cites Attac: the government brought this Senate debate forward, whereas the National Rally had planned to raise it on 10 December in its own parliamentary slot.

One version calls it "a licence for police to kill"; another calls it "not treating police as suspects every time they fire". The legal text itself says the presumption can be overturned, the conditions for firing are unchanged, and investigations still go ahead; but how the presumption will affect opening and closing cases in practice has no data yet.
Turnout also comes in two versions: 106,000 and 200,000, from the government and the organisers respectively, each with its own stake.

Presumed compliant first; can be overturned by contrary evidence

blocks.title: The 14 cases of 2024
blocks.text: The Senate report cites the General Inspectorate of the National Police: in 2024, 14 people died after police used their service weapons. In 12 cases the courts found the use lawful; the other 2 were still under investigation. The report concludes that the current framework is "very largely respected".

items: Firearms rules unified in Article L.435-1
Pauget and others table the bill
National Assembly passes the rewritten text
Nearly 50,000 march in about 100 towns against it
Union strike day, over 500,000 by official count
Senate law committee adopts it unchanged

critical.label: Another angle
items: Bill sponsors and the right (Droite Républicaine, National Rally)｜View: Police face ever more violence and need legal security.；Interest: Support from law enforcement, and the security issue.；Worry: Police being automatically treated as suspects after firing.；Basis: Assault figures cited in the Senate report; AFP: the National Rally says the bill prevents police from being automatically suspected of excessive force.

Senate law committee｜View: This is a rebuttable simple presumption that leaves the substantive rules intact.；Interest: Giving prosecutors firmer grounds to close cases when there is no evidence of misconduct.；Worry: The original "presumption of self-defence" would not fully secure officers' actions.；Basis: Rapporteur Josende's report of 10 Nov; committee adoption without change (Senate "L'essentiel" summary).

Student groups, unions and rights organisations｜View: This is a "licence to kill".；Interest: Holding police violence to account and protecting protesters.；Worry: Investigations harder to open, burden of proof falling on families.；Basis: Euronews quoting a student-union spokesperson; calls by Index, SAVE, the Human Rights League and Attac; a petition of 730,000+ signatures shelved.

The government and Macron's camp｜View: Under debt pressure, only limited concessions are possible.；Interest: Fiscal stability and public order.；Worry: A drawn-out street movement and further falls in popularity.；Basis: AFP: the government has little room to manoeuvre; unions called the +0.6% minimum wage "crumbs"; Index citing Attac: the government brought the Senate debate forward.

Young protesters and the injured｜View: They want teachers and safe school buildings, and they fear the police.；Interest: Learning conditions and personal safety.；Worry: The bill will make alleged police violence even harder to hold to account.；Basis: Euronews quoting high-school union leader Mesnil; France 24 quoting Adrien, a 20-year-old cellist; lawyers say at least 18 injured people will sue the interior ministry.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: The right and the National Rally push the bill from a security angle, while the government offers limited concessions on living costs (+0.6% minimum wage); in the same wave of street protests, demands about living costs and police powers have merged.
The Senate committee sees it as a simple presumption that leaves substantive rules unchanged; opponents fear the signal it sends: that a police shooting is assumed fine from the start.
Turnout is falling, while the unions' next strike (17 November) and the Senate debate (19 November) are only two days apart, putting the street and parliament on the same calendar.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The legal text says the presumption can be overturned and investigations continue; opponents fear cases will be closed more easily in practice. Neither claim yet has post-implementation data to test it.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Turnout comes with two counts, official and organisers', almost a factor of two apart.
The government's formal position on the bill itself is not clearly stated in the reports found for this article.
The outcome of the Senate debate and vote on 19 November was not known at press time; this article makes no prediction.
